articles.title: La cruda realidad de Bronny James
articles.standfirst: El base ha jugado menos de 10 minutos en lo que va de temporada, los Lakers han perdido por 25 con él en pista y ante los Raptors un parcial de 2-13 tras su salida casi les condena
articles.summary: El base ha jugado menos de 10 minutos en lo que va de temporada, los Lakers han perdido por 25 con él en pista y ante los Raptors un parcial de 2-13 tras su salida casi les condena
articles.body: Faltaban 2:28 para el final del partido y los Lakers ganaban por 123-107 a los Raptors. Con todo decidido, el entrenador JJ Redick hizo entrar a pista a Bronny James por Luka Doncic y a otros suplentísimos del conjunto angelino. En poco menos de dos minutos, la ventaja se había volatilizado. A 43 segundos del final, tras un parcial de 2-13, los titulares tuvieron que regresar a la pista. Austin Reaves ya le había regalado su toalla a un espectador y se la tuvo que reclamar. En lugar de aprovechar esos minutos, aunque fueran de la basura, los suplentes de los Lakers se condenaron al ostracismo. "No cometeré ese error de nuevo. Dejaré a los chicos en la cancha. Hay que jugar hasta el último segundo y si los suplentes no están listos para jugar, entonces simplemente no los pondré", lamentó Redick sobre la casi remontada de los Raptors. El suceso se podrá personificar en Bronny James, que suele ocupar uno de los últimos lugares del banquillo. Sólo ha jugado en tres de los siete encuentros de los Lakers y su papel siempre ha sido residual. En sus anteriores dos campañas en la NBA, ambas con papá LeBron cerca, había tenido una media máxima de 8,9 minutos. Ahora es todavía peor: 3,3. En total ha jugado sólo 9:51 minutos. En ese escaso tiempo en pista poco ha hecho: dos puntos, no ha atrapado ni un rebote, ni ha dado una asistencia y ha perdido dos balones. Ante los Raptors cometió una esperpéntica al botar fuera de las dimensiones de la pista el balón que iba a poner en juego en un saque de fondo. Pero lo peor es que, en los minutos que ha jugado esta temporada, ¡los Lakers han perdido por 25! En su tercera temporada en la NBA, se está haciendo aún más evidente que a Bronny (22 años y 1,88 metros) le va a costar encontrar un hueco en la competición incluso como especialista defensivo, que sería su faceta más destacada. En el horizonte aparecen dos posibles alternativas. Una es el traspaso y en las últimas fechas ha surgido la posibilidad de que entre en alguna operación como pieza complementaria para que los Lakers se refuercen. En otro contexto quizás él pudiera rascar algún minuto más. La otra es que siga en la franquicia angelina pero sea enviado al equipo vinculado en la G League. En una competición donde encaja mejor, promedió la temporada pasada 9,5 puntos, 3,5 rebotes y 4,5 asistencias en 30,8 minutos. En la NBA, visto lo visto, lo va a tener difícil.

articles.title: The Lakers 'live on a spaceship,' and Luka Dončić looks like the best damn pilot in the galaxy
articles.summary: The All-NBA playmaker has started the season on the kind of offensive heater that has the Lakers dreaming big.
articles.body:
Perhaps, while watching him flame-broil the Toronto Raptors on Sunday night to the tune of 45 points on 12-for-23 shooting with eight 3-pointers, you found yourself thinking, "Man, Luka Dončić is on an all-time heater to start the season."

Well, if it seems that way, it's because he very, very much is:

"You need three guys to guard him," Lakers big man Sandro Mamukelashvili said, according to ESPN . "I have a feeling that every time Luka plays, it's like 35-plus [points]."

Pretty close, Mamu. It's actually four times in six games this season. (The last four, if you're keeping score.)

Much of the postgame commentary about Dončić's performance in the Los Angeles Lakers' 131-125 win over the Raptors focused on his defensive work : on the 15 defensive rebounds he pulled down, on the five steals he snagged and six deflections he piled up, on the charges he took to draw offensive fouls and get the Lakers another possession. That certainly matters; Dončić is no stranger to catching hell for lacking defensive effort on the sport's grandest stage , and these Lakers will need him to put his best foot forward on that end if they hope to get back to that stage themselves.

"We've been relying on our offense a lot," Lakers center Walker Kessler told reporters after a loss to the Portland Trail Blazers last week. "And we have a very, very good offense and a lot of great scorers. But that's not gonna be the only thing that gets us to win a championship here."

It won't. It'll be the main thing, though. Because what the Lakers did, after ending the somewhat awkward stuck-between-stations stint that stretched from Dončić's arrival at the 2025 trade deadline and the team bidding farewell to LeBron James this summer, was build A Luka Dončić Team. And if there's one thing A Luka Dončić Team is going to do, it's score a truckload of points — with the lion's share of them coming off the fingertips of No. 77.

Sunday's monstrous performance against the Raptors made Dončić just the second player since the NBA began tracking steals in 1973 to score 45 points, collect 15 rebounds, dish 5 assists and grab 5 steals in a single game — joining, as luck would have it, Anthony Davis , the man whom the Lakers traded to Dallas to secure Dončić's services nearly two years ago. It was his 24th career 45-point game , tying George Gervin for 10th on the all-time list, and his 11th career 45-point, 10-rebound, 5-assist outing — more than anybody but Laker legends Wilt Chamberlain and Elgin Baylor.

Six times, Dončić has suited up for the Lakers this season; three times, he's topped 40 points. He is now averaging more than one point per minute — a historical rate of offensive onslaught that nobody has surpassed since Wilt did it 65 years ago .

This isn't normal. Luka just makes it seem that way.

"It feels like a supernova, but it also feels normal," Lakers head coach JJ Redick told reporters after Sunday's win. "We live on a spaceship and we're going at the speed of light at all times when he's on the court."

Dončić has opened the season looking like the best damn pilot in the galaxy, leading the NBA in scoring at 37.7 points per game, 8.1 points more than second-place Tyrese Maxey. That 8.1-point gap between first and second place is roughly the same as the gap between Maxey and Indiana Pacers forward Pascal Siakam, whose 21.4 points per game rank 28th in the NBA.

Dončić leads the NBA in made field goals per game, in 3-pointers made and attempted per game and in free throws made and attempted per game. He's converting on all those looks at or near career-best rates , shooting 78% at the rim, 53% from floater range, 47% on long-2 midrange looks, 90% from the free-throw line, and 43.2% from long distance. He's also tied for ninth in the NBA in assists, dishing 7.3 dimes per contest, making him one of two players in the top 10 in both categories, alongside Jayson Tatum of the Boston Celtics. Combine the points that Dončić is generating by setting up his big men at the rim and shooters on the perimeter with the ones that he's scoring himself, and he's creating 55.3 points of offense for the Lakers per game — most in the NBA, according to Databallr .

Including plays where he shoots or passes to a teammate who shoots, Dončić's pick-and-rolls are producing 1.18 points per play, the third-highest mark among players who've run at least 50 pick-and-rolls, according to Synergy Sports Technology's tracking. His isolations are generating 1.22 points per possession — fifth-best among players who've finished at least 20 one-on-one trips. When he orchestrates from the post, the Lakers have scored 1.36 points per trip — fourth-most among players to log at least 10 such plays.

Add it all up, and the Los Angeles offense has been an absolute buzzsaw with Luka at the controls. The Lakers have scored a scorching 130.7 points per 100 non-garbage-time possessions in Dončić's minutes ; as a point of comparison, the league-leading Rockets offense averages 122.1 . They're shooting the cover off the ball from everywhere with him on the floor : 80% at the rim, 58% from midrange and 43% from 3-point land.

They've been elite in the half-court , with Dončić poking and prodding and bending coverages until they snap. They've been even better in transition , where Dončić's combination of excellent defensive rebounding for a wing and perpetual eyes-up scanning for hit-ahead opportunities allow L.A. to get out and run into easy buckets:

"When he has it going, it's like, pick your poison, cause he can just make any shot," Redick said. "And then you start putting two on the ball, and everybody else is the beneficiary of that. He's a terrific offensive engine."

That engine is running red-hot to start the season, pacing the Lakers to a 5-2 record behind the NBA's No. 3 offense , with Dončić playing like an MVP frontrunner — and getting the help he needs from the Lakers' other core pieces.

Second banana Austin Reaves is averaging 23 points and five assists per game on 52/40/88 shooting. New center Kessler is holding up his end of the bargain, shooting a league-best 75.4% from the field, averaging 10 rebounds and 3 blocks per game, and holding opponents to a microscopic 41.3% at the rim when he's the closest defender; that's the best mark of any interior deterrent to face at least 25 up-close shots, according to Second Spectrum tracking .

All told, the Lakers have blitzed opponents by 84 points in 126 minutes with Dončić, Reaves and Kessler on the court together — the best point differential of any three-man unit in the league thus far — and their core lineups have largely been lights out, with a number of role players (Mamukelashvili, Ziaire Williams, Matisse Thybulle, et al.) providing the right kind of production and filling in the gaps around that high-priced, high-wattage core.

The spaceship could hit some turbulence, though. The Lakers have played one of the league's easier schedules thus far; three of their five wins have come against the Clippers and Jazz. They're also outperforming their expected field goal percentage to a higher degree than any other team in the league, according to multiple shot-quality metrics .

If that red-hot collective shooting normalizes — and if the ball-security issues that have L.A. ranking 28th in team turnover percentage , with Dončić and Reaves sitting first and second in the league in total cough-ups — then the Lakers could be in for some regression … especially if, y'know, Luka doesn't continue to average like 38 points per game on Prime Steph shooting and Prime Harden usage for a full season.

Of note: Luka's never gotten to the basket less. His 18 drives per game are the third - lowest average since entering the NBA, and a career-low 9% of his shot attempts have come at the rim, according to Cleaning the Glass . He's balanced that out by taking more than half of his attempts from 3-point land for the first time in his career, which is a pretty good idea when you're making them; what happens, though, if those stepbacks aren't cashing in at a 43% clip?

If and when that comes, some of those other shortcomings — the hole at power forward, the lack of another viable ball-handler to help Reaves buoy the offense when Dončić rests, the worrisome lack of rebounding and interior heft when Kessler's off the floor, etc. — could become more glaring. For now, though, the Lakers are off to what's been by and large a glass-half-full start: a top-three offense with a just-below-average defense , outscoring opponents by 7.5 points-per-100 (a 58-win pace ), with Dončić looking like the best player on the floor damn near every time he sets foot on it, somehow making the obscene look routine.

It doesn't seem possible that a spaceship like these Lakers can keep going at the speed of light without eventually slowing down. That's the thing about superstars like Dončić, though: When they've got it going, the limits of physics and history and even our imaginations can just seem to fade away.

"All of the great, great players that have ever played have also been in the 1% competitor [level]," Lakers assistant coach Greg St. Jean recently told Thuc Nhi Nguyen of the Los Angeles Times . "They've always been the guy that is able to inspire the players around him and be able to do things that don't even seem like they're possible. And he does that nightly."

articles.title: Russell Westbrook's Thunder Jersey Retirement Announced in Hype Video for NBA Legend
articles.summary: The Oklahoma City Thunder announced they'll retire Russell Westbrook's No. 0 jersey on Feb. 7, 2027.
articles.body:
The Oklahoma City Thunder announced they'll retire Russell Westbrook's No. 0 jersey on Feb. 7, 2027.

The nine-time All-Star will be the first player honored exclusively for his time in OKC.

Westbrook's rookie season was the Thunder's inaugural year in Oklahoma City in 2008-09. Across an 11-year period, he and the team went on quite the journey.

There was the Thunder's run to the 2012 Finals with Westbrook, Kevin Durant and James Harden and then the what-if created by Harden's exit the following offseason.

OKC remained a contender with Westbrook and Durant but couldn't advance past the Western Conference Finals in 2014 or 2016.

The Thunder's championship window slammed shut with KD's exit in the summer of 2016, but that allowed Westbrook to shine brighter than he ever had. He was the MVP in 2016-17 after averaging a triple-double with 31.6 points, 10.7 rebounds and 10.4 assists.

The fans' connection to Russ deepened as well because he was the star who stuck around.

General manager Sam Presti made one last roll of the dice by acquiring Paul George, which resulted in a pair of first-round exits. By the 2019 offseason, the writing was on the wall. George got traded to the Los Angeles Clippers, and Westbrook was routed to the Houston Rockets shortly thereafter.

The numbers speak for themselves as to Westbrook's overall contributions. Since the christening of the Thunder era, no OKC player has more points, rebounds, assists or steals than him.

articles.title: No. 1 South Carolina opens season with 101-93 win over No. 20 Maryland in Paris; Addi Mack scores 35 for Terrapins
articles.summary: The Gamecocks built too big of a lead to overcome, but Maryland's Addi Mack scored 31 second-half points in a star-making performance.
articles.body:
No. 1 South Carolina began its 2026-27 season looking like one of the best teams in women's college basketball with a 101-93 win over No. 20 Maryland on Monday at the Oui-Play event in Paris.

However, the Terrapins put up a fight in the second half and sophomore guard Addi Mack announced her arrival as potentially one of the top stars in the sport with 35 points, shooting 6-for-10 on 3-pointers.

The Gamecocks asserted themselves from the beginning, running out to an 8-0 start that eventually became leads of 15-2 and 22-5. South Carolina ended the first quarter up 33-14.

Dawn Staley's team didn't let up in the second quarter with Agot Makeer scoring nine points and Joyce Edwards tallying 13, including a buzzer-beating jumper to put South Carolina ahead by 28 points at halftime, 61-33.

However, Maryland battled back in the third quarter, fueled by Mack scoring 17 points in the frame. The Terrapins outscored the Gamecocks by nine in the quarter, though still trailed 78-59 going into the final 12 minutes.

An 8-0 run midway through the fourth quarter cut South Carolina's lead to 89-80 with just under five minutes remaining. But the Gamecocks scored the next seven points to restore their lead to 16 points at the three-minute mark.

Yet the Terrapins had one more run in them, going on a 10-0 streak powered by Mack and Bri McDaniel. Trinity Jones hit a 3-pointer to make the score 96-90 with 43 seconds remaining in regulation.

Jones was one of three Maryland players to score 11 points, while Nunu Agara tallied 12. Mack scored 31 of her points in the second half.

South Carolina put the game away with five free throws in the closing 30 seconds, three of them from Jerzy Robinson, who finished with 15 points and six rebounds. Edwards led the Gamecocks with 23 points and eight boards, followed by 20 from Makeer, who made all four of her 3-point attempts. Tessa Johnson also scored 15 points, adding six rebounds and five assists.

The Gamecocks are off until Sunday while traveling back to the United States. They will face No. 12 North Carolina in Charlotte as part of the Ally Tipoff doubleheader. Maryland's next game is also on Sunday, hosting George Mason.

The disclosure follows her appearance on Theo Von’s "This Past Weekend" podcast, where she said she believed the FBI was watching approximately 20 people over concerns involving her. articles.title: Longtime journalist and ESPN commentator Michael Wilbon is taking a leave of absence
articles.summary: Michael Wilbon, the longtime ESPN commentator and co-host of the network’s popular “Pardon the Interruption” talk show alongside good friend Tony Kornheiser, announced Monday he is taking a leave of absence because of what he described as “multiple health issues.”
articles.body: Michael Wilbon is taking a break. The longtime ESPN commentator and co-host of the network’s popular “Pardon the Interruption” talk show alongside good friend Tony Kornheiser announced Monday he is taking a leave of absence because of what he described as “multiple health issues.” Wilbon, who turns 68 later this month, wrote in a post on X that he is taking a trip to “the injured list” but added he hopes it is “not an extended one.” While Wilbon, who is also featured on ESPN’s NBA coverage, declined to go into detail about what he is facing, he added that there are people in his personal life who noticed “worrisome signs” in recent years that he largely ignored. Wilbon did make a point to note the issues are not alcohol or gambling-related. “I have no idea how exactly this part of my journey will wind up,” Wilbon posted. “The goal is to come out of it feeling much better than I do now and ready to return to sparring with Tony.” Wilbon’s last appearance on “PTI,” which recently celebrated its 25th anniversary and is credited with revolutionizing television’s “sports debate” format, was on Oct. 26. The show, in part, is a byproduct of the friendship of Wilbon and Kornheiser, who became colleagues at the Washington Post in the 1980s. “I have loved sparring and hosting PTI with Tony every single day these past 25 years,” Wilbon wrote. “And I’m incredibly grateful for the support and encouragement of my colleagues as I take this time away to concentrate on me, especially my well-being.”

articles.title: Un español en la cuna de Michael Jordan
articles.standfirst: El zaragozano Jorge Sanz cuenta sus primeros meses como ayudante de Mike Malone en la legendaria Universidad de North Carolina
articles.summary: El zaragozano Jorge Sanz cuenta sus primeros meses como ayudante de Mike Malone en la legendaria Universidad de North Carolina
articles.body: En la Universidad de North Carolina, la tercera más laureada en la historia del baloncesto universitario; donde jugó Michael Jordan, campeón en 1982; y a las órdenes de Mike Malone, ganador del anillo de la NBA en 2023 con los Nuggets. Ese es el entorno en el que habita Jorge Sanz, entrenador español que se ha labrado una dilatada y brillante carrera en la NCAA y también ha colaborado con la FEB trabajando con la ilusionante generación que ahora llega a la selección absoluta. El técnico zaragozano ejercerá este año como ayudante en los legendarios Tar Heels después de ocho exitosas campañas en Gonzaga (2018-26) con un balance de 238 victorias y 38 derrotas. Antes había estado otras ocho campañas en Florida Atlantic (2010-18), donde llegó desde España junto a la que acabaría siendo su mujer persiguiendo un sueño que no deja de crecer. En ambos programas de menos a más: de edición de vídeo, preparación de partidos y técnica individual, a reclutamiento internacional y a tener más incidencia en lo que pasa en la pista. Hasta que en mayo de este año recibió la llamada de Mike Malone. Todo un campeón de la NBA al teléfono. "Me contactó él directamente, pero un conocido común ya me advirtió que me iba a llamar. Me preguntó: '¿Si te llama Mike Malone, escucharías?'. ¡Pues claro que sí! Me dieron el aviso. A esta gente no le gusta fallar", relata Sanz en conversación con MARCA desde Chapel Hill, sede de la Universidad. Y desde el primer momento hubo buenas sensaciones con su jefe: "Conecta muy bien con la gente. Da importancia a las relaciones interpersonales y desde la primera llamada hubo un impacto. Sentí un interés real y genuino en conocer mi historia y mi trayectoria". En el tiempo que lleva trabajando con Malone le ha llamado la atención que "es muy detallista. Su nivel de preparación es muy alto para cada entrenamiento, reunión o partido" y también su intención de integrar a todos y generar buen ambiente. "Es exigente, pero no es trabajar en la obra. Entiende los momentos de distensión, de hacer piña. Es muy agradable el trabajo de esta manera", afirma Sanz. Él es uno de los siete entrenadores ayudantes. "Es como un club", asegura. Sus labores tiene que ver con el ataque. "A nivel técnico, estoy en la parte más ofensiva. También en desarrollo y técnica individual", explica. Cada uno de los entrenadores ayudantes trabaja con tres jugadores casi a diario para preparar vídeos, partidos y entrenamientos. Entre sus pupilos, el exazulgrana Sayon Keita, de 18 años y 2,16 metros. Además, Sanz se encarga del reclutamiento internacional. En su carrera ha llevado a 17 jugadores de nueve países. "La competición va de noviembre a abril, pero la gestión es todo el año. Somos nosotros quienes evaluamos y fichamos, viendo jugadores, hablando con agentes y las familias... Esto no para nunca", descubre. Sólo UCLA (11) y Kentucky (8) suman más títulos NCAA que los seis de North Carolina. "Es un orgullo y una responsabilidad estar aquí, donde la presión no viene ya sólo por ganar sino por hacer las cosas con una excelencia marcada de manera interna. Se transmiten la tradición y la historia", cuenta. Hay pósters, cuadros, camisetas colgadas del Dean Smith Center, con capacidad para 21.000 espectadores, que recuerdan los éxitos y a los mitos. Por encima de todos ellos, Michael Jordan: "Es un estandarte. Su figura tiene un impacto que se ha transmitido durante décadas. Es referencia a nivel histórico y deportivo por lo que fue aquí y por lo que ha sido desde entonces y lo que sigue siendo a nivel imagen". Entre su aventura en Estados Unidos, Sanz también ha colaborado con la Federación Española. Formó parte del cuerpo técnico encabezado por Javi Zamora que ganó las platas U17 en el Mundial 2022 y en el Eurobasket U18 de 2023. También estuvo en la concentración 'España Futuro' organizada por el seleccionador Chus Mateo con mucha presencia de jugadores de la NCAA. Por sus manos ha pasado el presente y, sobre todo, futuro del baloncesto español: Aday Mara, Hugo González, Sergio De Larrea, Izan Almansa... "Un honor representar a la selección y poder compartir pista y campeonatos con chicos de tanto talento y con tantas ganas de trabajar y de ganar. Formaron grupos muy especiales", dice quien considera que "es para tener esperanzas en el futuro. La materia prima está. Ahora deben seguir trabajando para creer como jugadores y personas. Los de la NBA van a llevar cada uno su ritmo, pero lo importante es que, largos o cortos, den pasos firmes".

articles.title: Trade Packages and Landing Spots for Sacramento Kings Star Domantas Sabonis
articles.summary: Just under four years ago, Domantas Sabonis was the best player on a Sacramento Kings team that looked ready to establish a winning culture after decades of incompetence.
articles.body:
Just under four years ago, Domantas Sabonis was the best player on a Sacramento Kings team that looked ready to establish a winning culture after decades of incompetence.

He led the Kings to the playoffs in 2023, and they've steadily declined ever since.

It's early, but this season, they look like maybe the only safe pick to wind up in the league's new "relegation zone" (the bottom three records have a worse shot at the No. 1 pick than the teams with the fourth- through 10th-worst records).

And before they get there, it looks like Sabonis may want out.

Whether he's explicitly told the team that or not, if Sacramento makes Sabonis available, there are teams that should be interested.

Since he joined the Kings five-plus years ago, Sabonis has averaged 18.9 points, 13.1 rebounds and 6.9 assists. He comes with real defensive concerns, but the 2022-23 Kings proved you can work around those.

Below are some realistic moves that would put him on teams that would do just that.

Kings Receive: CJ McCollum, Luguentz Dort and a top-eight protected 2029 first-round pick

The Atlanta Hawks are loaded with length and athleticism. And at least in theory, that should help them rebound, but it hasn't translated to much more than mediocre numbers in that category the last two seasons.

Sometimes, you need more brute strength and sheer size, and that's exactly what Sabonis would add.

Counting this season, he's led the league in rebounds per game in four of the last five seasons. And while his defense has been a problem in the past, Jalen Johnson, Dyson Daniels and Nickeil Alexander-Walker are the kind of athletes on the perimeter who could protect him.

Pairing his passing with Johnson's would also give the Hawks one of the most dynamic playmaking frontcourts.

They'd lose some leadership and three-point shooting by including CJ McCollum in this deal. And Luguentz Dort has been a solid addition to the defense. But Kingston Flemings already looks more ready for real responsibility than anticipated. Aaron Wiggins has been a boost to the guard and wing depth. And Onyeka Okongwu may be mobile enough to spend some time alongside Sabonis.

For the Kings, this is mostly about getting a pick, but McCollum and Dort might also be good vets for Darius Acuff to develop around. The former could help Acuff know how and when to pick his spots offensively, and the latter could impress the importance of perimeter defense on him.

Kings Receive: Draymond Green (trade-eligible on December 15), Kristaps Porziņģis, Will Richard and a top-four protected 2032 first-round pick

The Golden State Warriors' better-than-expected start makes a Draymond Green trade harder to imagine, but they look like a near-ideal landing spot for Sabonis, and they simply can't get him without including Green or Jimmy Butler.

The more logical approach, assuming the Warriors really want to chase one more title with Stephen Curry, is to pair Green's salary with the Kristaps Porziņģis contract, which was essentially designed to be a human trade exception.

The math still doesn't quite work with those two, so Will Richard is also essential, but this is still worth it for Golden State.

Sabonis would be a dramatic upgrade over Green in scoring and rebounding. He's at least as good a passer (though maybe not quite as good a creator). And it's easy to imagine the fit between him and Yaxel Lendeborg. Curry's off-ball movement around either (or both) of those interior hubs would be nearly impossible to stop.

It's maybe a harder sell on the other side of the deal. Neither vet seems like a longterm option for Sacramento, but Green's deal is expiring and Porziņģis' is only guaranteed for $3 million. They represent an opportunity for flexibility, while Sabonis' deal is guaranteed for $48.6 million next season.

That, a flier on 23-year-old Will Richard and a protected draft pick for someone who'll be on his way out in 2028 anyway is good value.

Kings Receive: Jalen Green, Mark Williams (trade-eligible on January 15) and Rasheer Fleming

The Phoenix Suns' draft assets are essentially spent, but Sacramento may struggle to extract unencumbered first-round picks from anywhere.

And if that's the case, this is a deal the Kings could talk themselves into, especially if Sabonis is planning to walk away in 2028.

It lands the Kings a talented (though flawed) scorer in Jalen Green, who's around eight months older than Yaxel Lendeborg and another upside play in Rasheer Fleming.

Mark Williams is mostly here to match salaries, but his contract runs through 2028-29 and pays him no more than $14 million. He could be another good trade chip down the line.

This framework is easier to understand for Phoenix. Sabonis is six years older than Green (and eight years older than Fleming), but he's on the same timeline as Devin Booker and plays a game much more likely to lift the Suns' star than Green's.

This deal obviously wouldn't push the Suns to immediate title contention, but a starting five of Collin Gillespie, Booker, Dillon Brooks, Miles Bridges and Sabonis would make Phoenix a tough out.

articles.title: BOBBY BURACK: The anti-white resistance is already beginning for Cooper Flagg
articles.summary: Cooper Flagg's rise as a 19-year-old Dallas Mavericks star is sparking a heated racial debate after ex-NBA player Charlie Villanueva's comments.
articles.body: Dallas Mavericks forward Cooper Flagg is 19 years old and already one of the best basketball players in the world. Last week, ESPN analyst Jeremy Lin called him "generational" and said he and Victor Wembanyama could become the NBA’s next great rivalry. Flagg has also drawn favorable comparisons to LeBron James at the same age, including from Brian Windhorst. "In my view, Cooper is better at defense than LeBron was at the same age. I don’t even think it’s debatable," Windhorst said. "There were defensive plays LeBron made at that age. He certainly would get into passing lanes, he certainly would block shots, he was a defensive playmaker, but Cooper is better defensively, empirically; I don’t think that’s debatable." Flagg is averaging 27 points, six rebounds and seven assists during his second season. A phenom of Flagg’s caliber should be a gift to the NBA as some of its biggest stars, including LeBron James, Steph Curry and Kevin Durant, approach the end of their careers. Instead, his rise may expose the worst instincts in sports. Cooper Flagg is White. For some members of the basketball community, that is a problem. Former NBA player Charlie Villanueva is one of them. Villanueva discussed Flagg’s rising stardom on the "To The Baha" podcast last week. According to Villanueva, Flagg cannot become the face of the NBA because of his skin color. "This might sound crazy, but I don’t think in 2026 a White dude could be, I’m gonna be real, could be the face of the league, if I’m being honest," Villanueva said. "Because it’s a Black league, right?" EMBRACE OF WEMBY AS FACE OF THE NBA PROVES RESISTANCE TOWARD JOKIC WAS ALWAYS RACIAL | BOBBY BURACK He then argued that a White player cannot become the best player in the NBA. "When is the last time we’ve seen a White man be the face of the league? Don’t say Larry Bird, they had to pair him up with Magic," Villanueva said. "When was the last time a White man was single-handedly the best player in the league?" That talking point was predictable. OutKick predicted it days after Flagg became the first overall pick out of Duke last season. DAKICH: SPORTS MEDIA HAS CREATED AN ‘INDUSTRY’ OUT OF COMPLAINING ABOUT WHITE ATHLETES LIKE CAITLIN CLARK For the past three to four years, several former Black players comfortably expressed belittling views of White players. The hysteria surrounding Caitlin Clark began with the claim that her popularity and stardom resulted from "White privilege." Black players have called Luka Doncic a "bitch ass white boy" on the court. ESPN analyst Kendrick Perkins falsely accused NBA MVP voters of favoring Nikola Jokic because he is white, likely costing him the award in 2023. More recently, Stephen A. Smith claimed a team could not win a championship built around white players. Former broadcaster Mark Jones has posted several bigoted messages about Jokic. Gilbert Arenas has joked about exiling white players from the league. ESPN has published several articles framing Jokic, Clark, and Doncic as "great white hopes," despite the evidence to the contrary. The pattern is obvious. Anti-white bigotry has become accepted and, at times, rewarded in public discourse. It has been normalized since 2020. Notice Villanueva’s wording: The NBA is "a Black league, right?" STEPHEN A SMITH SHOWS HIS PRIVILEGE BY MOCKING LAKERS' ROSTER FOR HAVING TOO MANY 'WHITE DUDES' That view echoes comments from Arenas and others who refer to the NBA as "our" league. These Black players appear territorial about the sport and seem threatened when white players succeed. For context, consider what activist and social media influencer Dr. Umar Johnson said about Eminem in 2023. Johnson claimed Eminem should be excluded from the conversation about the greatest rappers of all time because of his skin color. "No non-African can ever be the best of anything African. It’s an insult to the ancestors. It’s an insult to the race and it’s an insult to every black person." Johnson then claimed the black community should never have allowed Eminem into hip-hop. "Eminem has all the privileges of a white male and all the privileges of being in the hip hop community, so we got to be careful about letting non-Africans into our community." That is the message Black players send about White basketball players: Basketball is their sport. White people are merely their guests. Of course, the premise is illogical. Basketball is not a black space. A White man created it. No sport or musical genre belongs to any race in America. The popularity of both White and Black athletes and entertainers makes that clear. Normal Americans like Eminem for the same reasons they like Tupac, Biggie, or Jay Z. They like Jokic, Clark, Doncic, and Flagg for the same reasons they like LeBron James, Michael Jordan, and Kobe Bryant. Unfortunately, people with the largest platforms too often promote an isolated worldview in which race determines who deserves admiration, legitimacy, and power. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Flagg could prove particularly polarizing. The usual suspects tried dismissing Jokic and Doncic as international players. Flagg does not give them that option. He was born in Maine. He attended Duke. His charismatic personality also gives him marketing potential that Jokic and Doncic lacked. If Flagg emerges as a true face of the post-LeBron NBA, expect the race idolaters to react accordingly. They will resist him and diminish him with the usual racial buzzwords. They will cast his supporters as racists and sellouts. Sound familiar? Of course, it does. It's the response every great white basketball player now receives. For Flagg, Villanueva's comments were just the beginning.

articles.title: JuJu Watkins drops 21 points in long-awaited return from ACL injury to lead No. 3 USC past UNLV in opener
articles.summary: JuJu Watkins missed all of last season recovering from an ACL injury she suffered during the 2025 NCAA tournament.
articles.body:
After spending roughly 19 months away recovering, JuJu Watkins finally made her official return to the court Monday afternoon in Las Vegas.

Watkins led No. 3 USC to a blowout 100-68 win over UNLV to officially kick off the 2026-27 campaign at T-Mobile Arena. It marked her first real outing since she tore her ACL during the NCAA tournament in 2025.

Watkins dropped 21 points and shot 9 of 22 from the field in the dominant outing. She dropped 11 points in the third period alone, while the Trojans outscored UNLV 31-10 to blow the game wide open. Watkins did miss all five of her attempts from behind the arc.

"It was great to just be out there with my team again, and to see the first one fall through, it really helped," an emotional Watkins said on the court. "Just grateful to be out here today … Just so many hours went into this, just really grateful that I'm at this point."

Her first bucket came midway through the opening frame, when she drove and made an and-1 layup through Jasmyn Lott down low. She followed that three-point play with an easy layup just seconds later, too.

Jazzy Davidson added 23 points and shot 10 of 11 from the field for the Trojans. Saniyah Hall finished with 22 points and seven rebounds.

Watkins went down in the second round of the 2025 NCAA tournament during the Trojans' win over Mississippi State. She was driving to the rim on a fast break and collided with a pair of Bulldogs players before crashing to the court awkwardly. She had to be helped up and carried off the court.

Quickly, USC ruled her out with an ACL injury. That's kept her sidelined ever since, and she ended up missing all of last season recovering .

Watkins averaged 23.9 points and 6.8 rebounds per game during the 2024-25 season while earning consensus national player of the year honors. The Trojans were a No. 1 seed in the NCAA tournament that season, and ended up losing to UConn in the Elite Eight. The Trojans went 18-14 without Watkins last season and reached the second round of the tournament, their fourth straight appearance under head coach Lindsay Gottlieb.

While it was a long time away, Watkins made the most of it.

"I think my injury let me reset and remind myself why I do what I do and why I love it so much," Watkins told ESPN's Kendra Andrews before the season-opener. "These days [my why] is a lot of knowing I've gone through such a long period of not being able to do what I love and just being present in the moment and grateful for how far I've come. "The pressures will always be there. I pray that the pressure gets even higher because that's a privilege."

"These days [my why] is a lot of knowing I've gone through such a long period of not being able to do what I love and just being present in the moment and grateful for how far I've come.

"The pressures will always be there. I pray that the pressure gets even higher because that's a privilege."

Watkins came to USC as the No. 1 recruit in the country, and she's widely considered to be the top pick in the WNBA Draft next spring should she decide to make the jump. The expectations of her leading USC to a national championship, something the school hasn't pulled off since 1984, are absolutely still there.

"I feel like her impact on us is probably more palpable than ever before," Gottlieb told ESPN . "I know when I had her freshman and sophomore year, well, shoot, you got a player like that, you are going to be in conversations to be great. But now it feels more."

It's still very early in her return, and there are several notable tests coming up before Big Ten play gets going — including a battle with No. 1 South Carolina on Nov. 15.

But Watkins is back, and has picked things up right where she left off.

articles.title: Zion Williamson Leads NBA Steals As Pelicans Find New Rhythm
articles.summary: Zion Williamson leads the NBA in steals while the Pelicans dominate the Hawks. Jamahl Mosley sees a clear path to winning with this defensive identity.
articles.body:
They crushed the Atlanta Hawks 121-99 on Halloween night to secure their second straight victory. This performance was a stark contrast to their 0-4 start that left fans worried about the season. Zion Williamson is now the top player in the entire league for steals. He is averaging 3.2 steals per game according to The Advocate. That number puts him ahead of every other defender in the NBA right now. The Pelicans are leading the league in steals per game as a team, according to the Advocate . They grabbed 15 steals against the Hawks alone.

Jamahl Mosley has always been known for his defensive coaching skills. He is finally seeing his vision come to life on the court. He noted that Zion is sitting down and guarding instead of just gambling for balls. The coach told The Advocate that Zion is leading the league in steals while being positional. He is not chasing the ball but is in the right spot at the right time. This aggression makes the offense much easier for the whole team. The Pelicans scored 34 points off Atlanta turnovers in this game. They also held the Hawks to just 38.5 percent shooting from the floor. The team is now ranked fourth in the league in defensive rating. That rating sits at 104.0 points allowed per 100 possessions. Mosley was pleased with the energy and toughness his guys showed all night. He said the team's effort was plentiful.

The starting lineup was changed for New Orleans. Herb Jones returned to the starting five and he is the most dependable defender on the roster. Coming off the bench against his former team, Saddiq Bey recorded four steals. Bryce McGowens and Trendon Watford are also getting minutes and bringing length. The starting group of Fears, Jones, Murphy, Williamson, and Matkovic has won back-to-back games. Every single player in that lineup finished with a plus-14 rating or better. Jeremiah Fears stepped up with 20 points, five rebounds, and seven assists. He hit a lob to Williamson; a scuffle and a loud crowd reaction occurred. The Pelicans will try to make it three straight wins when they face the Memphis Grizzlies on Monday night. The Grizzlies are still the only undefeated team in the NBA at 6-0. Zion Williamson is not celebrating his lead yet though. He told The Advocate to ask him again around Game 20. He wants to see if he is still top five then. If he is, then they are doing good.

articles.title: How Natalie Nakase and the Valkyries built  a championship franchise at light speed
articles.summary: Some have taken to calling Nakase a “basketball sicko.” She calls herself an “obsession extremist.” Regardless, everyone can now refer to her as a championsh...
articles.body:
Natalie Nakase pings around the practice courts at Sephora Performance Center in Oakland the day before the WNBA Finals begin, setting screens, throwing up a hand to contest shots and cheering encouragement on missed shots.

Everything she does is quick. Talk quickly. Do quickly. Live quickly. She's the type of person who is always on to the next, blinders to the ultimate task to the point she doesn't eat and lacks sleep. But she never looks at or shares her Oura ring's readiness score. She doesn't have to, she insists, because she's always ready.

Some have taken to calling her a "basketball sicko." She calls herself an "obsession extremist."

"I can keep doing the same thing over and over again until I get amazing at it, until I perfect it," Nakase said. "And so that's maybe why I felt like I could perfect the perfect game plan, that I could win it right away."

Ahead of Game 1, she carried the mentality that winning could come quickly. It wasn't a characterization of her opponent, the Atlanta Dream, whom she praised for an incredible season. It was one of herself.

But in her first Finals as head coach, it was all too much. Not the stage or the pressure or the task ahead. Her. She was too much. Her quick approach wasn't working. The Valkyries eked out a Game 1 Finals victory in comeback fashion, but lost back-to-back games with uncharacteristic performances she graded as F-. They needed to win Game 4, and Nakase needed to find a new way.

She took a breath. Her mentors are always on her about that. She reflected. In film sessions she described as vulnerable and honest, the two-time WNBA champion as an assistant with the Las Vegas Aces listened closer to players about what they saw and needed. She adjusted, speaking slower and more clearly about the game plan.

The Valkyries responded with a fresh starting lineup, holding the Dream to season-low offensive games in each of Game 4 and Game 5. After dropping Game 6, she tapped back into the process and drilled down the sense of urgency it takes to win in what was officially their last attempt.

It completely changed the series, more than any tweak or in-game adjustment either head coach could make. And she couldn't have done it if there wasn't a foundation already built around it that extended beyond her hiring. Golden State is the rare WNBA champion to have summited immediately, both as a franchise in its second season and a core of players that had yet to make a deep playoff run together. The Valkyries proved defense wins championships, showed that offense could be optional if it was good enough and most importantly that making the right hires and signings underlines it all.

"Y'all think I know what I'm doing?" Nakase asked for the second time in three days, this time in celebratory Champagne goggles and a soaked championship T-shirt. "I just switch things just to switch it up. You think it's some science behind it. It really isn't. It's just literally just to mix it up."

Whether there's a science that other teams can successfully repeat — and they will now try — remains to be seen. But clearly, Nakase and Valkyries brass know exactly what they're doing.

Valkyries principal owner Joe Lacob, when on the stage accepting the trophy and surrounded by reporters near a courtside VIP room celebration, took every opportunity to credit the trio of women who executed what many thought a far-fetched mission.

But he can't fully pull himself out of it. He did hire them, after all.

Months after the WNBA awarded Golden State Warriors co-owners Lacob and Peter Graub the league's first expansion franchise since 2008, Lacob brought on Jess Smith in January 2024 as the team's first president. Her prior experience covered sports start-ups, coming over from a position as head of revenue for the NWSL's Angel City Football Club since its inception in 2020.

While Smith dove into designing and marketing a team that has sold out every game in existence and became the first women's sports team to generate $100 million in revenue, Lacob poached Ohemaa Nyanin from the New York Liberty as the Valkyries general manager. As an assistant GM, Nyanin helped build the Liberty's superteam in 2023 that reached the Finals and won the championship in 2024.

This would be a different type of task. The Liberty, at the time, were the only original franchise to have not won a title. They used a No. 1 overall pick on Sabrina Ionescu and added All-Stars around her, leveling up to Nakase's former Aces and their three consecutive No. 1 selections.

The Valkyries weren't in a position to do that. And that drought wasn't going to cut it for Lacob. Not even close. He told anyone who would listen, and probably those who didn't, he intended for the Valkyries to win it all within five years.

When he told Nakase in her head coaching interview, she one-upped him.

"I was like, yes, that's going to happen," Nakase said. "But even faster."

Nakase and Nyanin bonded early and worked closely to build their inaugural roster through an expansion draft, selecting a group of 11 that leaned heavily into defense and international talent and fit the culture they prioritized. Four of the Valkyries selected in their expansion draft are still rostered; Veronica Burton (Sun), Kayla Thornton (Liberty) and Cecilia Zandalasini (Lynx) all started in the Finals. Iliana Rupert (Dream), the intended starting center, missed the season on maternity leave.

They left their first free agency without a bang, a partial result of players waiting to assess the expansion squad and awaiting collective bargaining negotiations. The most notable acquisition was reigning Sixth Player Tiffany Hayes, whom Nakase asked to "take a leap of faith" with her from the Aces so she'd have a familiar face.

With the No. 5 pick in their first collegiate draft in 2025, the Valkyries selected Lithuanian guard Justė Jocytė and in the third round, UConn point guard Kaitlyn Chen. Chen, who played four years at Princeton, wasn't dressed for the draft; she was there to support UConn teammates, including No. 1 pick Paige Bueckers.

The Valkyries reached the playoffs in their inaugural season, becoming the first WNBA team to accomplish that feat. As the No. 8 seed, they lost to No. 1 Minnesota in a first-round sweep. Nakase won Coach of the Year and Veronica Burton, a Northwestern grad and Wings first-round draft pick who was waived ahead of season tipoff, earned Most Improved Player.

It was clear from the beginning the team was designed in the likeness of Nakase, a former UCLA walk-on who dreamed of playing in the WNBA. The inaugural defense led the league (76.3 ppg allowed) with the offense lagging behind nearly everyone (77.7 ppg ranked 10th). She balanced her team's minutes and rotations, remembering from her NBA career how health could interrupt a championship run.

As much as she asks questions of her players, she does the same with her mentors as well. Tyronn Lue, for whom she coached with the Clippers, won early in his head coaching career. Joe Mazzulla won his second year in Boston, and like Nakase didn't play in the respective league. They instilled in her two key pieces of advice that she leaned on more than any stat.

"First, just build a culture of competitors, but love, as silly as that sounds," Nakase said. "But having a culture that really wants to fight every single day, players that really want to fight every day, but also feel psychologically that safety, and that's that love and care that you have to provide."

To hack away at this premise that love leads to winning is akin to questioning that the Earth is round. Yes, Nakase genuinely believes her players love each other. They've all endured previous roster cuts or bad situations, and most were left unprotected by their prior teams to be selected by the Valkyries. There is a level of trauma bonding, she said, that has led to quick chemistry. They wouldn't undercut each other like that.

"When you allow them to come in and be who they are, I think it's something magical," Kayla Thornton, a top reserve on New York's 2024 title team, told Yahoo Sports before the series. "This is what our team is built off of: a lot of women that never had the opportunity, never were put in the right position, and now that we are, it's something great."

Nakase asks to be enlightened as to what's beyond love.

The WNBA career of Gabby Williams, a two-time NCAA champion at powerhouse UConn, is one defined by a lack of trust and connection. To see the good side of it up close is what drew her into Nakase's and Golden State's fold.

Williams initially met with Valkyries brass in 2025 free agency, opting to stay in Seattle on a one-year deal. When she met with Nakase and general manager Ohemaa Nyanin again in March as a 2026 unrestricted free agent, she noted how many players returned. And she felt a difference in the meeting.

"I could see how much closer they had gotten in just that year, and their back and forth," Williams said. "That tells me something about their culture, too, and how personable they are with each other. That was a green flag for me."

Williams signed a three-year, $3.7 million deal as Golden State's splashy offseason addition that would fit seamlessly on the defensive end. Offense was more of a question mark; she never averaged more than 12 points per game, though she earned her first All-Star honor in 2025.

The Valkyries also signed three-time Aces champion Kiah Stokes with the intention she would back up Rupert. Life had other plans, and Stokes stepped up while Rupert had her first child. The veteran UConn champion stonewalled four-time MVP and former teammate A'ja Wilson in the semifinals sweep and Dream forward Angel Reese the majority of the Finals. The $761,000 salary is proving to be a steal , and Stokes joined seven players all time with four championship rings. Rebekkah Brunson has a record five.

In the Bay, they both feel appreciated after being overlooked or left aside. It was pivotal for Williams, who learned firsthand what Nakase was trying to establish.

"The team already had a culture and relationships established," Williams said. "But I walked into a group full of love and that just changed the entire trajectory of my career."

Williams was drafted by the Chicago Sky with a 2018 lottery pick and four years in, communicated her intent to play in the 2021 Tokyo Olympics. It was her first opportunity for the senior national team, a special moment as her mother is French and she holds dual citizenship. Nothing lights up Williams in a media environment more than a question in French.

She missed training camp for the Olympics, and the Sky suspended her for the season. She requested a trade that was granted, but never played for the Los Angeles Sparks while with the French national team. In February 2022, the Sparks traded her to the Storm, where she won three All-Defensive honors and finished third in Defensive Player of the Year in 2025 while becoming the face of the league's prioritization clause under the previous CBA .

She's now the face of the Finals and by extension the league. Her 30 points in Game 7 tied the league record, and 28 of them were scored in a second-half takeover that put the Dream on their heels. Lacob described it as legendary. Nakase called their closer "f***ing incredible," even though she hadn't realized the point total by the time they sat down as champions.

"To me the MVP is the Finals MVP," Nakase said. "You have to play through the playoffs, you have to grind, you have to go through a seven-game series. She's the Most Valuable Player in the world, hands down."

There was institutional support to reach that level Williams had never experienced. When she needs someone to watch her cat, Halle Berry, Nyanin helps find someone. It doesn't matter if it's a road trip or Williams needing time to prioritize rest and recovery. Nakase is always focused on player health, and the season-long care of her roster – even during a FIBA World Cup year – was a pivotal, overlooked aspect of Golden State's title run.

It's not merely the team's No. 1 on the scouting report who receives such star treatment. Nyanin is part general manager, part assistant, because that's what it takes to build rapport and success. If there's an everyday life pain point she can solve, she'll do it. Everyone matters to the Valkyries, and everyone receives what they or their loved ones need to best perform.

"She's not just taking care of 14 people," Nakase said. "She's taking care of a whole community, and I think that's really special."

There's an intentionality that everyone within the organization appreciates. It goes all the way to Smith and her team's selection of the specific shade of violet that drapes Chase Center, Stoke said. The merchandise stands in and out of the arena are branded "Golden State." Even the ropes in the back of the house are Valkyries violet. A sewer cover on the north side of the arena is painted the same color, easily hidden in a planter's box.

None of that matters if Nyanin and Nakase couldn't select the right group of "egoless" players who took on regular-season games like hockey lines. The bench set a scoring record, averaging 35.9 points per game on a team that collectively averaged 82.2, better than only the Connecticut Sun.

"If I was just gonna start a new franchise, I think I would try to go that route where any given night it could be someone's day," Stokes said. "I think that's harder to scout because you're not focusing on taking away like one or two people."

The defense reached another level, becoming one of the best units in league history. Janelle Salaün won Sixth Player of the Year unanimously, but factored out of Finals rotations. Nakase faced the difficult decision to play seven in the latter stages of the series, but all were ready to go. Three different players led the team in scoring during the Finals. Five different ones led a game in rebounds. Another four in assists.

It allowed Williams, the newbie, and Stokes, who is running out of ring room, to stand slightly above the rest and bring an early championship home to Ballhalla.

Williams looks at the box score, the full room of reporters, the WNBA championship trophy. And then she realizes she might have this wrong.

The fresh championship flat brim goes on backwards. Or at least, four-time champion Stokes and three-time champion Nakase are wearing theirs backward.

"I've never done this before," Williams said, flipping the hat and re-donning the Champagne goggles. "Is this how I'm supposed to do it?"

The hat is less important than the alcohol, of which Williams has none. Nakase — always aware of her players — is on top of it, lightly encouraging Stokes to later pass the bottle.

This is a vastly different version of Nakase than the one 17 days ago, flurrying between practice courts. She clinks an aluminum beer bottle to Stokes' bottle of wine as a French reporter asks a question of Williams. Nakase drops f-bombs with aplomb, despite earlier in the series appearing horrified she accidently let one slip on the podium. There is no talk of failed messaging or film. She is a rare sight of patience with no immediate plans of leaving.

"Girl, I just need to get drunk tonight, so let me get there," Nakase said, brushing off talk of repeating. "Let's enjoy the moment."

Lacob, watching from the side, earlier in the night ducked questions of whom he would be calling during free agency. Former MVP runner-up forward Napheesa Collier, second-highest scorer Kelsey Mitchell, two-time Aces champion guard Kelsey Plum and three-time Aces champion Jackie Young are all unrestricted free agents. The postseaon matchups in a wonky season that included a late World Cup break allowed the Valkyries to get away with a highly limited offense. That won't always be the case.

Maybe if they had lost, that would be top of mind. But right now, all he's thinking about is enjoying an "insane" championship two years into existence in front of a Ballhalla fanbase already topping the league.

"I'm not really good at enjoying things for too long, but winning's fun," said Lacob, whose Warriors won four championships in eight years. "I don't know if you noticed."

By sunrise, Valkyries championship banners featuring each player's likeness lined the Embarcadero. They will celebrate a championship parade there Wednesday following a private ceremony in Oakland.

Nakase will begin obsessing again soon, intent on doing it all again quickly.

articles.title: Braden Smith starting for severely short-handed Pacers vs. Hawks
articles.summary: The Pacers have just seven players truly available for Monday's game vs. the Hawks, so former Purdue star Braden Smith will start.
articles.body:
Former Purdue All-American and Westfield High School star Braden Smith will start for the severely undermanned Pacers on Monday in the second night of a back-to-back against the Hawks for his first start as an NBA player, coach Rick Carlisle said in his pre-game news conference Monday.

Smith, a second-round pick on a two-way contract, has played 18 minutes in four appearances. He's 0 of 3 from the floor, but has scored one point on a free throw. The all-time assists leader in Division I history has registered two assists.

"This is obviously a great opportunity for Braden," Carlisle said. "He will start so he'll have his first career NBA start which is pretty exciting for him I would think."

The Pacers will dress just eight players with seven of the actually available. Forward Obi Toppin, who was listed as questionable when the injury report was released Monday afternoon, will dress to give the Pacers the required minimum number of eight active players but he will not play, Carlisle said. Forward Larry Nance Jr., listed as doubtful with an illness, will also not play.

Eight other players were ruled out in Monday's initial injury report. All-Star forward Pascal Siakam, forward Aaron Nesmith and guard Andrew Nembhard are sitting out the second half of a back-to-back for rest or injury management reasons. Carlisle noted that this was the Pacers' second back-to-back in a week which is why the players got this day off and not the second night of the season's first back-to-back. All Star point guard Tyrese Haliburton (left hamstring strain), center Ivica Zubac (left ankle sprain), backup point guard T.J. McConnell (right hamstring strain), guard Ben Sheppard (torn left meniscus) and forward Johnny Furphy (torn ACL) have all been out for multiple games with their injuries and are still out.

Of the seven healthy and available players, just four are on standard contracts -- guard Quenton Jackson, forwards Kelly Oubre Jr. and Jarace Walker and center Jay Huff. All three players on two-way contracts -- Smith and forwards Kobe Brown and Jalen Slawson -- have to be active.

"We're just gonna have to get through this thing the best we can," Carlisle said.

articles.title: Valkyries offer WNBA, other Bay Area teams lessons on supporting fans, winning with grace
articles.summary: While the WNBA was on the front line of the country's culture wars, the Golden State Valkyries stayed true to their fans and themselves. The league and other...
articles.body:
Thirty-six hours after they flung their exhausted bodies toward each other in celebration, after they lifted a trophy and drank champagne and finally ate some food and were feted at a Warriors game and dug through their text messages (including one from Michael Jordan) and got some sleep, what they had accomplished was still hard to process.

"It hasn't really hit yet," Kayla Thornton said Monday morning, sitting beside the silver WNBA Championship trophy that was still waiting to be engraved with this phrase:

It's going to take days, months, maybe years, to process the full impact of what these women, this team accomplished.

But some lessons are immediately obvious.

First of all, the Valkyries have taught the entire Bay Area sports world how to do it: how to be inclusive and represent the very best of the Bay Area. How to welcome all fans, sprinkle joy via sports, and make the community feel connected and invested and welcome. There's a baseball team down the street from Chase Center whose players should sit down with the Valkyries for a lesson on how to fully represent our diverse, unique land.

As Natalie Nakase said, "Sports is about belonging. It's about inclusivity. It's about allowing everyone to be their authentic self."

After a win on Valkyries Pride Night, Gabby Williams joyously shouted, "This is for the gays!" She frequently said that Ballhalla "became my safe space." And she needed that sanctuary this season.

When Fever player Sophie Cunningham and clowns like Enes Kanter Freedom helped turn the WNBA into a toxic battleground over the nonexistent – but politically flammable – issue of transgender women in the league, Williams caught shrapnel. Someone unearthed an innocuous quote from earlier in the season when Williams said "I would welcome a trans athlete on my team or against my team anytime. I don't think it's a problem in the world. It's just another way to attack trans people." It got posted on social media, months later and out of context, and Williams was suddenly in the cross-fire of the culture wars.

On Monday, Williams said she would never stop fighting for those who can't always fight for themselves but acknowledged that voicing her belief was "scary."

"I was getting death threats, there were some security issues and there were moments when I was like, 'How are you doing this?' and then I would walk into Ballhalla and say 'Oh that's how, that's how.'" she said. "So I want to thank our fan base for just being themselves because it allowed me to be myself and that's huge. This is what the Bay Area is all about. The Bay Area is the pioneer in these kinds of issues and topics. So I'm proud to represent the Bay."

The Valkyries also sent a clear message to the rest of the WNBA about how to build and run a team. They gave a master class on not only what is possible, but what should be expected. No more second-class citizenship. No more half-assing it. The Valkyries raised the bar for the entire league.

Get out of those rinky dink arenas – that includes the three-time champion Aces who play in an auditorium in the bowels of a casino – and get deals with the real arenas in your cities. If we learned anything from the ridiculous saga of the location and timing for the Atlanta Dream home games during this Finals series, it's that fans will show up for the product even with only a few days' notice.

And, for God's sake, hire women. For too long, the people who run WNBA teams have plugged men into the top jobs because they didn't have the will or connections to find top women to run their teams. In the women's collegiate game, as the prestige grew and the jobs became more attractive, we've seen men taking the plum jobs and pushing women out. The same should not happen in the rapid acceleration of the W's profile and profitability.

Joe Lacob deserves a ton of praise for hiring three brilliant women for all of his top jobs: president Jess Smith, general manager Ohemaa Nyanin and Nakase as head coach. None had held those positions before. All have excelled, to put it mildly, in their roles.

Also: Expand the playoffs, and get rid of the dumb "best of three" first round. This was the first time a WNBA Finals went seven games and it was compelling theater every step of the way.

"Seven games is a long series," Kiah Stokes said. "To play the same team seven times in a row is tough mentally and physically. My body hurts so bad right now. It was grueling, it was physical, it was tough. And once it's over and you take a step back you realize, damn, everything hurts."

The ratings for Game 7 weren't out yet when the Valkyries were speaking, but they're sure to be great.

"My rookie year, we were wearing shirts that said 'Put Women's Sports on TV,'" Stokes said. "We just needed to get attention. So to actually be able to showcase what we can do when we get attention and have a great product on the floor, that shows what we can accomplish."

The Valkyries also taught a lesson in togetherness. Tiffany Hayes said it was unlike anything she'd ever seen before in her 14 years in the league.

"Just that type of camaraderie in that time span," she said.

The connectivity went throughout the organization.

"I'm so proud of this whole organization, all the people in this building that helped us through the season, coming to work with a smile every day and making us feel safe and understood," Cecilia Zandalasini said. "It's just a great joy to share this with everybody."

Veronica Burton said she was most proud of the way the Valkyries won their championship.

"I think we won with grace, and lost with grace and that's not easy to do in these moments because you don't know what the outcome is going to be," Burton said. "I think our attitude and approach never shifted. And who we are and our character never wavered.

"We won and lost with a lot of grace and a lot of love."

articles.title: Russell Westbrook’s wife Nina has a special message after Thunder make franchise-changing decision about his No. 0 jersey
articles.summary: The Oklahoma City Thunder will retire Russell Westbrook’s No. 0 jersey on Feb. 7, 2027, when they host the Knicks.
articles.body: The Oklahoma City Thunder will retire Russell Westbrook’s No. 0 jersey on Feb. 7, 2027, when they host the Knicks. General manager Sam Presti announced it Monday at the team’s Day One Luncheon, and Westbrook wiped away tears on stage as the news landed. The club followed with a video montage of the Oklahoma City years. His wife, Nina, was among those who reacted online, along with former teammates. The honor arrives a few months after the 18-year veteran announced his retirement in August.Nina reacts as Thunder set date to retire Russell Westbrook’s No. 0Nina posted her message in the comments under the Thunder’s Instagram announcement. “Zero my hero,” she wrote, followed by a heart. Her comment came after her husband heard the news live from the stage.Westbrook will be the second player in Thunder history to have a number retired, after Nick Collison, whose No. 4 went up in 2019. Oklahoma City drafted the nine-time All-Star in the first round in 2008, and he spent 11 of his 18 seasons there.Carmelo Anthony, Westbrook’s former teammate in Oklahoma City, kept his response brief, writing, “Deserved.”Westbrook’s road out of Oklahoma City and back to the raftersThe Thunder traded Westbrook to Houston ahead of the 2019-20 season as the team rebuilt. Washington, the Lakers, the Clippers, the Nuggets and the Kings followed. He was named to the NBA 75th Anniversary Team in 2021 and retired this offseason with nine All-Star nods.Oklahoma City is where his numbers peaked. Alongside Kevin Durant, he helped turn a young roster into one of the league’s best teams, and when Durant left in free agency after 2015-16, Westbrook’s role grew. In 2016-17 he won MVP while averaging 31.6 points, 10.7 rebounds and 10.4 assists, the first full-season triple-double average since Oscar Robertson. He left as the franchise’s all-time leading scorer with 18,859 points.Presti tied the decision to more than stats. “Many players have an impact, but only great players leave a legacy,” he said in a statement. The general manager said Westbrook built that legacy on the court and in the community, and that people across Oklahoma see him as family.Speaking to reporters, Westbrook called the news “a true blessing.” He said he never imagined growing up that he would reach the NBA, and that a retired jersey reflects the time, effort and energy he put into the game. articles.title: No. 1 Florida passes biggest test of NCAA's opening day with stifling win over No. 14 Miami
articles.summary: Thomas Haugh led Florida's offense in the season opener after bypassing the NBA Draft, while Florida's defense smothered Miami's attack.
articles.body:
No. 1 Florida and No. 14 Miami faced off in the only top-15 matchup of Monday's opening day of the college basketball season.

The top-ranked Gators passed the test in convincing fashion at the Tampa site of their stunning second-round NCAA tournament exit to Iowa last season. The top-ranked Gators stifled the Hurricanes on defense and fought off multiple Miami flurries to start their season with a quality 77-67 win .

It marked a strong start for a Florida team that enters the season as the favorite to secure its second national championship in three seasons.

A Miami team that's projected to challenge No. 2 Duke for ACC supremacy got off to a good start and took a 17-15 lead in the game's opening minutes. Florida responded with a 9-0 run for a 24-17 lead that it extended to 41-27 late in the first half.

Miami cut the deficit to as close as three points early in the first half and mounted multiple runs late, but the Gators never relinquished the lead. A Thomas Haugh bucket in transition off one of many Miami misses extended Florida's lead to 71-62 late, and the Hurricanes never threatened again.

Haugh, who returned to Florida despite projections as a first-round NBA Draft pick, paced the Gators with 19 points, 10 rebounds and 4 assists. He hit 4 of 8 3s to lead an offense that was uneven at best in its first game of the season.

But it was more than enough next to a shutdown defensive effort that limited Miami to 1-of-19 shooting during a late second-half stretch.

As a team, Miami shot 21 of 60 (35%) from the field and 4 of 17 (24%) from 3. Preseason first-team All-ACC selection Shelton Henderson was limited to seven points and nine rebounds on 2-of-13 shooting from the field.

Instead, it was sophomore Villanova transfer Acaden Lewis who led the Hurricanes with 24 points on 9-of-20 shooting as Miami's most reliable offensive weapon.

For Florida, Boogie Fland (12 points, 4 assists) and Alex Condon (11 points, 7 rebounds) were the only players not named Haugh in double figures. The Gators shot 43.4% from the floor and 42.3% (11 of 26) from 3.

Florida takes on another in-state rival in Florida State on Nov. 10 and will face Notre Dame on Nov. 17. But it won't face another ranked opponent until a Dec. 1 showdown against Duke.

Miami's next games against ranked opponents are scheduled for Dec. 2 against No. 20 Alabama and Dec. 12 against No. 7 Texas.

Wilson is making a strong case for Rookie of the Year, but the Bulls' 1-6 start to the season indicates that they likely won't be a playoff team just yet.

articles.title: Who was Erin Benavides? Revisiting her connection to Tony Parker and Eva Longoria after tragic news
articles.summary: Erin Benavides, a former Texas prosecutor once at the center of an NBA scandal, has died by suicide at 54.
articles.body: Erin Benavides, a former Texas prosecutor once at the center of an NBA scandal, has died by suicide at 54. According to TMZ, Police found her dead at a home in Port Aransas on Oct. 14 after a friend of her husband alerted them to a worrying text message she had sent. The news came out this week and brought fresh attention to the 2010 claims linking her to Spurs star Tony Parker, who was married to actress Eva Longoria at the time. Benavides denied the affair. The investigation is still open, and police do not suspect foul play.Erin Benavides and her alleged link to Tony ParkerBenavides first made national headlines in 2010. She was married to Brent Barry then, who was Parker’s Spurs teammate from 2004 to 2008. Barry divorced her and alleged an emotional affair with the six-time All-Star. Longoria reportedly found hundreds of text messages from another woman on his phone, later identified as Benavides. Benavides denied the affair, and Parker reportedly denied any physical contact.Both marriages ended. Benavides and Barry had been married since 1998 and split in 2010. Longoria filed for divorce in November of that year, and the two divorced in 2011. The actress later told Extra that Parker had also cheated earlier in their marriage.Erin Benavides’ career and work for childrenBenavides later built a career in law. She worked as an assistant district attorney in Texas’ 38th Judicial District, which covers Uvalde and Real counties, from January 2023 until she resigned in August 2026. Her work was in the anti-gang and border prosecution unit.Outside the courtroom, she focused on children. From 2020 to 2022, she was president and CEO of the Youth Center of Texas, which offers crisis intervention and case management to child sex-trafficking victims. Yolanda Valenzuela, executive director of Kym’s Angels Foundation, also recalled her work with the Bexar County Child Welfare Board, where she helped run mass-adoption ceremonies and a Christmas fundraiser that bought gifts for local foster children.District Attorney Christina Mitchell paid tribute on Facebook. Mitchell said Benavides brought laughter and energy to the office and often spoke with pride about her sons. “Her boisterous laugh throughout the office will be greatly missed,” Mitchell wrote. articles.title: "Un blanco no puede ser la imagen de la NBA. Mi primera vez fue con una blanca, por lo que no soy racista"
articles.standfirst: El exjugador Charlie Villanueva sostiene que un jugador blanco como Cooper Flagg no puede ser la imagen de la NBA y trata de justificar su opinión tras las críticas
articles.summary: El exjugador Charlie Villanueva sostiene que un jugador blanco como Cooper Flagg no puede ser la imagen de la NBA y trata de justificar su opinión tras las críticas
articles.body: Charlie Villanueva, jugador de Raptors, Bucks, Pistons y Mavericks de 2005 a 2016, fue muy criticado al asegurar que Cooper Flagg no puede ser la cara de la NBA debido a su color de piel. "Puede sonar a locura, pero, siendo sincero, no creo que en 2026 un tipo blanco pueda ser la imagen de la NBA. Al fin y al cabo, es una liga de jugadores negros, ¿no?", comentó el número 7 del Draft de 20055. Antes las críticas recibidas Charlie Villanueva (42 años) publicó un vídeo en X (Twitter) para tratar de desmarcarse de las acusaciones de racismo. "Estoy diciendo hechos. Tengo ojos; simplemente digo lo que veo. La NBA es, ¿qué? ¿Predominantemente qué? Gracias. Alrededor de un 70-75 % son negros, un 20 % blancos, y el resto son, quizás, latinos, asiáticos u otros. Dicho esto, ¿estoy equivocado por decir algo así? Ustedes probablemente dirían lo mismo", subrayó. Según el 'Informe sobre Raza y Género de la NBA' de 2023, el 82,5 % de los jugadores durante la temporada 2022-23 eran personas de color. El ala-pívot de 2,11 m., que fue internacional con República Dominicana, apuntó que "es como la NHL. La NHL es, ¿qué? ¿Predominantemente qué? Gracias. ¿Llegará a haber alguna vez un hombre negro que sea la cara de la liga? Espero… Exacto, a eso voy. Entonces, ¿estoy loco por pensar así? Díganme qué opinan". Aunque Villanueva se refería a ser "la imagen de la NBA" varios creadores de contendidos malinterpretaron sus palabras, asumiendo que quería decir que un jugador blanco no podía ser el mejor de la NBA. Por ello, Villanueva tuvo primero que aclarar estos comentarios en sus redes sociales. "¡Un momento! Eso no es lo que dije. Luka Doncic y Nikola Jokic son dos de los mejores jugadores del mundo, a pesar de ser internacionales. ¡Y Cooper Flagg es de élite! Mi argumento trataba sobre quién es la cara de la NBA, no sobre quién puede ser el mejor jugador. Son dos temas completamente distintos" matizó. Charlie Villanueva, en el podcast 'To The Baha', se reafirmó en su postura: "¿Cuándo fue la última vez que vimos a un hombre blanco ser la cara de la NBA? No me digan Larry Bird; tuvieron que emparejarlo con Magic Johnson. ¿Cuándo fue la última vez que un hombre blanco fue, por sí solo, el mejor jugador de la liga?". "¿Alguna vez han entrado en una sala y se han dado cuenta de algo como: "¡Caramba!, soy el único tipo negro aquí"? O tal vez el 70 o 75 % de las personas en la sala son negras... o blancas. Y uno piensa: "¡Vaya!", explicó. El jugador de origen dominicano insistió en que "en la NBA, entre el 70 y el 75 % de los jugadores son negros. Y luego están los blancos —lo digo tal cual es—, que son quienes dirigen la liga, ¿no? Todos los propietarios son blancos. Sí; judíos, blancos, o como sea que quieras llamarlo, ¿verdad?. Es impensable que, en un entorno donde el 70-75 % de los integrantes son negros, se permita que una persona blanca sea la cara de la liga. Pero esto no es ninguna falta de respeto hacia Cooper Flagg; Cooper es un buen chico". En un momento de las charla Charlie Villanueva sintió la necesidad de abordar posibles acusaciones de racismo contra las personas blancas mencionando su historial sexual. "Mi primera vez fue con una chica blanca. Todos recordamos nuestra primera vez, ¿verdad? Entonces, ¿por qué iba a ser racista?", dijo dejando a todos los contertulios atónitos
